claim: Heights and reduction. (1) The heights lemma (proved). In the split at the attachment point the merged face takes one skip, on the arc fixed by the port class, so the class fixes the ports' height differences exactly; the heights with those port values are the integer solutions of a difference system, closed under rounded midpoints, so each point's height ranges over an interval of integers and its value is fixed exactly when its height is. So a port pattern freezes exactly the points whose height difference to the ports cannot vary. Checked: 102 of 102 port patterns fix the ports' heights, 488 of 488 frozen (point, pattern) pairs have a fixed height difference, and 4,752 of 4,752 (line, pattern) pairs agree with the transfer, on a ladder, a grid, a grown space, a thick tube and a ladder arm spliced onto a grid. (2) The reduction lemma (proved for the transfer and the pipeline). Across a 3-edge cut, a side holding neither the attachment point nor the gluing line acts as the vertex it lost, so replacing it by that vertex leaves the transfer and the pipeline's creation unchanged, with the handle's ports on corresponding lines. Checked at every attachment point of two rings spliced onto the 64-point grid and four small junctions: 253,536 (line, removal, far side) cases with no disagreement; exactly (join method) on the 21-point junction, 1,080 cases. (3) So the faces-around-the-point law holds in the reduced space: all 554 creating far lines on the point's side lie on a face around it there, including the 28 off those faces in the spliced space, the junction counterexample of FACE-CLAIM-20261103-001C. A ring point sees the closed prism, where the ring's far face is its opposite face.
